name: CHILD syndrome
aliases: congenital hemidysplasia with ichthyosiform naevus and limb defects

clinicalPearls: Acronym for Congenital Hemidysplasia with Ichthyosiform naevus and Limb Defects, characteristically strikingly lateralised (one side of the body)
The ichthyosiform erythroderma stops abruptly at the midline and typically follows the lines of Blaschko, with a waxy yellowish scale
Ipsilateral limb hypoplasia or defects and skeletal stippling (chondrodysplasia punctata) are hallmark associations
Caused by mutations in NSDHL, an X-linked dominant gene in the distal cholesterol biosynthesis pathway, and is lethal in most affected males
Ptychotropism (a predilection for skin folds) is a distinctive feature of the naevus
Ipsilateral visceral, cardiac, renal and central nervous system anomalies may accompany the cutaneous and limb findings
Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics; topical cholesterol-pathway (statin/cholesterol) preparations have been used to target the metabolic defect
reference.pathophysiology: CHILD syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in NSDHL (NAD(P)H steroid dehydrogenase-like protein), an enzyme acting in the distal (post-squalene) cholesterol biosynthetic pathway. The gene is X-linked, and the disorder behaves as an X-linked dominant trait that is generally lethal in hemizygous males, so affected individuals are almost always female. Random X-inactivation (lyonisation) produces functional mosaicism, which explains the sharply lateralised, Blaschko-linear distribution of skin and limb involvement. Deficient cholesterol synthesis and accumulation of toxic sterol precursors impair epidermal barrier formation and normal morphogenesis of limbs and viscera on the affected side.
additionalDifferentials: Conradi-Hunermann-Happle syndrome (X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata, EBP)
Ichthyosis with confetti and other mosaic ichthyoses
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing psoriasiform hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis and a characteristic verruciform xanthoma-like dermal infiltrate
Molecular genetic testing for NSDHL mutations
Radiographs for chondrodysplasia punctata (epiphyseal stippling) and limb defects
Echocardiography and renal imaging for ipsilateral visceral anomalies
Neuroimaging where central nervous system involvement is suspected
Sterol profiling to demonstrate distal cholesterol-pathway abnormality
redFlags: Cardiac or renal malformation causing functional compromise in the neonate
Extensive erythroderma with barrier failure and risk of infection or dehydration
Progressive scoliosis or limb dysfunction requiring orthopaedic intervention
Central nervous system anomaly with neurological deterioration
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends chiefly on the extent of internal organ and skeletal involvement rather than the skin disease. The cutaneous naevus persists lifelong but is compatible with a normal lifespan when major visceral malformations are absent; associated cardiac or renal anomalies are the main determinants of outcome.
pitfalls: Mistaking the lateralised naevus for a simple epidermal naevus or psoriasis and missing the syndromic limb and visceral defects
Failing to screen for internal anomalies once the cutaneous diagnosis is made
Overlooking the diagnosis in a male, in whom it is rare and often lethal or associated with mosaicism
Assuming skin-directed therapy alone is sufficient without multidisciplinary evaluation
management: Pathogenesis-based topical therapy for the ichthyosiform naevus combining a statin with cholesterol, to replace the deficient product and reduce accumulation of toxic sterol precursors
Skin-barrier care with emollients and keratolytics, giving particular attention to the hyperkeratotic skin folds affected by ptychotropism
Orthopaedic and reconstructive management of ipsilateral limb hypoplasia and defects, with mobility aids or prostheses
Assessment and management of ipsilateral cardiac, renal and central nervous system anomalies, which chiefly determine prognosis
Ophthalmology and other specialist input directed by the pattern of visceral involvement
Multidisciplinary care across dermatology, clinical genetics, orthopaedics and relevant organ specialists
Genetic counselling for X-linked dominant, male-lethal NSDHL disease, with family assessment
